talks.title: Security Analysis of the Telegram IM
talks.teaser: Security Analysis of the Telegram IM
talks.summary:
### Telegram Architecture and the Roll-Your-Own Crypto Dilemma
At 00:00, Tomas Susanka opens with an evaluation of Telegram, an instant messaging platform boasting hundreds of millions of users that promotes itself as a fast and secure communication tool. Susanka highlights the immediate red flag raised by the cryptographic community: rather than adopting established, peer-reviewed primitives like TLS or the Signal Protocol, Telegram engineered its own proprietary transport and end-to-end protocol dubbed MTProto.

### Default Cloud Chats vs. Opt-In Secret Chats
At 03:15, Susanka distinguishes between Telegram's default "Cloud Chats" and its optional "Secret Chats." In standard cloud chats, messages are encrypted only between client and server using MTProto; plaintext message histories, media, and encryption keys reside directly on Telegram's cloud servers. Only "Secret Chats" provide true end-to-end encryption (E2EE) where keys remain solely on endpoints, but this mode must be manually initiated and does not synchronize across multiple user devices.

### Cryptographic Anatomy of MTProto 1.0
At 07:22 and 10:37, the presentation dissects the cryptographic building blocks of MTProto 1.0. Susanka critiques Telegram's idiosyncratic design choices, including the pairing of SHA-1 hashing with non-standard AES in Infinite Garble Extension (IGE) mode. He demonstrates that MTProto lacks modern authenticated encryption (AEAD) primitives like AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. By computing message authentication over plaintext rather than ciphertext, MTProto fails to achieve IND-CCA (indistinguishability under chosen-ciphertext attack) security.

### Practical Vulnerabilities and Replay Attacks
At 14:08 and 17:30, Susanka outlines practical attack scenarios against the MTProto protocol. He reviews how subtle implementation flaws allow active network adversaries to manipulate message padding, stage replay attacks, and observe timing side channels. Furthermore, he points out that Telegram's phone-number-based authentication leaves users vulnerable to SS7 cellular intercept attacks and SMS hijacking, which bypass client-side protections unless two-step verification is enabled.

### Security Recommendations and Protocol Evolution
Concluding around 20:04, Susanka evaluates subsequent updates (including MTProto 2.0) that phased out SHA-1 in favor of SHA-256 and improved MAC validation. Nonetheless, he warns security-conscious individuals against relying on non-standard cryptographic designs, advising users requiring provable end-to-end privacy to utilize fully open, mathematically audited messaging platforms.

talks.title: The Key Management Facility of The Root DNSSEC
talks.teaser: The Key Management Facility of The Root DNSSEC
talks.summary:
### The Root DNSSEC Trust Anchor
At 00:00, Punky Duero introduces the role of ICANN (Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers) in maintaining the integrity of the global Domain Name System. He explains the architecture of DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC), where the Root Zone Key Signing Key (KSK) serves as the universal cryptographic trust anchor for the entire Internet hierarchy, cryptographically authenticating DNS responses and preventing cache poisoning.

### Inside the Key Management Facilities (KMF)
At 04:12 and 08:25, Duero provides a rare glimpse into the physical Key Management Facilities located in Culpeper, Virginia and El Segundo, California. Operating as geographically redundant bunkers, these facilities are engineered to resist physical intrusion, electromagnetic eavesdropping, and environmental disasters. Security controls include biometric iris scanners, seismic detectors, continuous video surveillance, and electromagnetic Faraday shielding protecting the ceremony room.

### The Cryptographic Ceremony and Ceremony Roles
At 12:08, the presentation details the meticulous execution of quarterly root key signing ceremonies. To ensure that no single person or government can compromise the root key, the ceremony enforces strict M-of-N split knowledge and dual-custody controls. Roles are divided among ICANN staff, internal auditors, and external Trusted Community Representatives (TCRs)—independent cryptographers and Internet operators selected globally who hold physical smart cards in tamper-evident security bags to activate the Hardware Security Modules (HSMs).

### Hardware Security Modules and Tamper Verification
At 16:30 and 20:15, Duero walks through the physical hardware utilized during ceremonies, focusing on FIPS 140-2 Level 4 certified Hardware Security Modules (such as Thales e-Security nShield HSMs). These appliances zeroize cryptographic key material upon detecting physical drilling, temperature fluctuations, or enclosure tampering. Every step of the ceremony follows a publicly published script, broadcast live via streaming video and verified by third-party auditors.

### The Historic Root KSK Rollover
Concluding around 24:12, Duero discusses the historic first rollover of the Root Zone KSK (moving from KSK-2010 to KSK-2017). He outlines the technical complexities of updating the trust anchors on recursive resolvers across millions of autonomous systems worldwide, explaining how automated update protocols (RFC 5011) and extensive telemetry monitoring ensured global DNS stability without breaking Internet resolution.

talks.title: Cryptanalysis in the Time of Ransomware
talks.teaser: Cryptanalysis in the Time of Ransomware
talks.summary:
### The Inversion of Cryptography in Ransomware
At 00:00, Mark Mager opens by describing how ransomware fundamentally inverted the historic purpose of cryptography: instead of protecting sensitive data from unauthorized interception, adversaries weaponize strong encryption algorithms to deny legitimate users access to their own files. Mager explains that while modern ransomware groups aspire to build bulletproof cryptographic pipelines, author errors frequently open doors for malware analysts to recover data without paying ransoms.

### Common Implementation Blunders and Weak PRNGs
At 07:15 and 13:40, Mager classifies historical cryptographic flaws observed across ransomware families. Early and amateur malware authors routinely made catastrophic implementation mistakes, such as seeding Pseudo-Random Number Generators (PRNGs) with predictable system parameters like `time()`, `GetTickCount()`, or thread IDs. When seed entropy is constrained, cryptanalysts can brute-force the generation state across a narrow temporal window, mathematically reconstructing the symmetric decryption keys.

### Key Storage, Hardcoded Secrets, and Memory Artifacts
At 21:16, Mager demonstrates binary reverse engineering in IDA Pro to inspect cryptographic subroutines. He highlights cases where malware authors left hardcoded AES or Salsa20 symmetric keys inside binary strings, utilized static initialization vectors (IVs) across multiple files, or failed to zeroize plain keys in volatile memory prior to terminating the encryption process. Analysts can extract these memory remnants by inspecting system hibernate files, pagefiles, or crash dumps.

### Hybrid Cryptosystem Flaws and Flawed Asymmetric Wrappers
At 28:50 and 34:20, the presentation explores the hybrid cryptographic model adopted by sophisticated strains, which pair symmetric stream or block ciphers for high-speed file encryption with public-key asymmetric algorithms (like RSA-2048 or Curve25519) to encrypt the symmetric keys. Mager analyzes vulnerabilities arising when authors incorrectly implement RSA padding, generate small prime factors, or accidentally transmit client private keys back to command-and-control (C2) servers over unencrypted HTTP channels.

### Constructing Custom Decryptors and Incident Response
Concluding from 38:10 to 41:00, Mager details the process of writing automated, standalone file decryption utilities. He outlines incident response workflows for infected enterprises: immediately isolating hosts to preserve volatile memory, capturing network traffic for unencrypted key exchanges, and verifying file integrity headers before applying recovery tools to prevent irreversible file corruption.

talks.title: Have You Seen My Naked Selfies Neither Has M
talks.teaser: Have You Seen My Naked Selfies Neither Has M
talks.summary:
### Interpersonal Privacy and Domestic Digital Surveillance
At 00:00, Lauren Rucker addresses a critical yet frequently overlooked privacy paradigm: interpersonal privacy within intimate relationships, contrasting broad societal surveillance ("US vs. THEM") with relational surveillance ("ME vs. YOU within US"). She explores the psychological and technological dynamics where trust breaks down, leading romantic partners, spouses, or family members to weaponize personal electronic devices against one another.

### The Proliferation of Stalkerware and Dual-Use Surveillance
At 08:30 and 14:15, Rucker examines the commercial marketplace for "stalkerware" and covert spouse-monitoring applications. She details how commercial software marketed as parental monitoring tools or anti-theft tracking apps is repurposed for intimate partner abuse. Once installed, these tools run stealthily in background processes, intercepting text messages, logging keystrokes, activating device microphones, and tracking real-time GPS locations without the device owner's knowledge or consent.

### Physical Device Access and Authentication Loopholes
At 21:17, the presentation explores how relational proximity bypasses conventional technical security models. Spouses and domestic partners often possess physical access to target phones, know backup PINs, or register secondary biometric profiles (such as adding their own fingerprint or facial data). Furthermore, synchronized cloud accounts (such as iCloud Keychain, Google Drive, or shared family billing plans) expose sensitive personal photographs, browsing histories, and location breadcrumbs without requiring advanced malware.

### Legal Protections, the Wiretap Act, and Legal Grey Areas
At 29:40 and 35:20, Rucker analyzes the legal landscape governing domestic electronic surveillance. While federal statutes like the Wiretap Act and the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) explicitly prohibit unauthorized interception and access, prosecuting intimate partner surveillance remains notoriously difficult due to ambiguous claims of shared ownership or implied consent. She highlights the specific legal vulnerabilities faced by teenagers and minors whose parents exercise legal authority over their mobile contracts (around 41:15).

### Technological Hygiene, Safety Planning, and Remediation
Concluding the presentation, Rucker presents practical safety planning and remediation guidelines for victims of domestic surveillance. She outlines steps for auditing linked devices on cloud accounts, identifying hidden administrative profiles on mobile operating systems, enforcing hardware-based two-factor authentication, and securing personal communications through isolated burner devices when escaping abusive domestic situations.

talks.title: Rustls   Modern Fast Safer TLS
talks.summary:
### The Need for Memory Safety in TLS Stacks
At 00:00, Joseph Birr-Pixton introduces Rustls, a modern open-source Transport Layer Security (TLS) library written entirely in Rust. He explains that traditional C and C++ TLS implementations, most notably OpenSSL, have historically suffered from severe memory safety vulnerabilities—such as buffer overflows, use-after-free bugs, and out-of-bounds reads exemplified by the catastrophic Heartbleed vulnerability. Rustls was engineered to eliminate these bug classes by construction through Rust's strict compile-time ownership and borrowing rules.

### Radical Feature Pruning and Removing Legacy Cryptography
At 05:40 and 10:15, Birr-Pixton explains Rustls's deliberate design philosophy of radical feature reduction. Unlike OpenSSL, which supports decades of obsolete cryptographic algorithms and obscure RFC extensions, Rustls deliberately drops legacy ciphers. It omits insecure primitives like RC4, DES, 3DES, MD5, and SHA-1, as well as vulnerable block cipher modes like CBC mode that are susceptible to padding oracle attacks. Rustls focuses exclusively on modern AEAD ciphers—specifically AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305.

### State Machine Verification and Cryptographic Primitives
At 15:25, the speaker details the internal state machine of Rustls. He discusses handling AEAD nonces securely, avoiding nonce reuse in GCM modes, and enforcing cryptographic state transitions through Rust's algebraic type system. By relying on `ring` for underlying cryptographic operations and `webpki` for X.509 certificate path validation, Rustls avoids implementing raw math routines in-house, significantly minimizing cryptographic implementation risk.

### Performance Benchmarking Against OpenSSL
At 21:10 and 26:05, Birr-Pixton presents extensive benchmark comparisons between Rustls and OpenSSL. Across multiple metrics, Rustls achieves comparable or superior handshake throughput and lower latency, while consuming significantly less memory per connection. Furthermore, because Rustls optimizes memory layout and eliminates dead legacy code paths, server instances can scale to hundreds of thousands of concurrent TLS sessions with minimal memory footprint.

### Future Protocols and TLS 1.3 Readiness
Concluding at 30:42, Birr-Pixton discusses the trajectory of Rustls as the Internet transitions to TLS 1.3. Because TLS 1.3 standardizes 1-RTT handshakes, forward secrecy by default, and encrypted handshakes, Rustls's minimalist architecture provides a clean, robust foundation for embedding secure communications into production infrastructure, browsers, and embedded systems without the historical baggage of C-based stacks.

talks.title: The Symantec SSL Debacle Lessons Learned
talks.teaser: The Symantec SSL Debacle Lessons Learned
talks.summary:
### The Genesis of the Symantec SSL Distrust Crisis
At 00:00, Jake Williams introduces the unprecedented cryptographic controversy surrounding Symantec's Certificate Authority (CA) business. In early 2017, Google Chrome and Mozilla announced intentions to distrust all SSL/TLS digital certificates issued by Symantec and its subsidiaries (including Thawte, GeoTrust, and RapidSSL). Williams outlines how this confrontation shook the global Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) ecosystem, threatening to break secure connections for over 30% of the encrypted web.

### Uncovering Misissuance Through Certificate Transparency
At 09:45 and 17:20, Williams details the discovery of unauthorized test certificates, including a rogue certificate for `google.com` issued without Google's consent. While Symantec initially characterized the incident as an isolated internal testing mistake, security researchers analyzing public Certificate Transparency (CT) logs uncovered a pattern of systemic compliance failures. Symantec had outsourced certificate issuance to third-party registration authorities (CrossCert and others) without adequate oversight, resulting in thousands of misissued or improperly validated certificates.

### Browser Root Store Power and Architectural Conflict
At 25:37 and 33:10, the presentation examines the geopolitical and corporate tensions between browser vendors and established commercial CAs. Williams explains that major browser vendors (Google, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft) control the trusted root stores on billions of endpoint devices. When browser maintainers determined that Symantec repeatedly failed to comply with CA/Browser Forum baseline requirements, they leveraged their root store authority to force accountability upon one of the largest security conglomerates in the industry.

### The Remediation Plan and DigiCert Acquisition
At 40:15, Williams reviews the complex technical compromise developed between Google and Symantec. Rather than terminating trust abruptly—which would have incapacitated enterprise banking, e-commerce, and federal web portals—the browsers established a phased distrust timeline across Chrome releases. This forced Symantec to divest its entire web security and PKI division, resulting in DigiCert acquiring Symantec's CA infrastructure to rebuild validation processes from scratch.

### Strategic Lessons for Enterprise PKI and Web Security
Concluding between 46:30 and 51:16, Williams outlines practical takeaways for security architects and system administrators. He emphasizes that enterprises must automate certificate lifecycle management (via ACME protocols), enforce continuous Certificate Transparency monitoring, and eliminate single-CA dependencies to ensure operational continuity when major trust anchors are deprecated.

talks.title: Alice and Bob are Slightly Less Confused
talks.teaser: Alice and Bob are Slightly Less Confused
talks.summary:
### The Historic Failure of Usable Cryptography
At 00:00, David Huerta opens by revisiting the perennial crisis in cryptographic usability, referencing the classic 1999 study "Why Johnny Can't Encrypt." For decades, privacy software like PGP and GPG required everyday users to navigate arcane concepts: public/private key pairs, keyrings, fingerprint verification, trust metrics, and manual email plugin configurations. Huerta argues that security models that offload cryptographic decision-making onto non-technical users inevitably result in abandoned tools or catastrophic user error.

### Progress in Automated End-to-End Encryption
At 07:18 and 11:45, Huerta highlights the massive usability breakthroughs achieved over the preceding two years. Modern communication platforms—most prominently Signal, WhatsApp, and iMessage—successfully democratized strong end-to-end encryption by making cryptographic key exchange completely invisible to end users. By integrating identity keys into phone numbers and automating Diffie-Hellman ratchets, these platforms secured billions of conversations without requiring users to understand underlying cryptographic algorithms.

### Visual Verification, Safety Numbers, and Mental Models
At 15:11 and 19:30, the presentation examines how modern user interfaces communicate cryptographic integrity. Huerta analyzes visual fingerprint verification, showing how 60-digit hexadecimal fingerprints were replaced by scannable QR codes and numerical "Safety Numbers." He discusses how intuitive visual cues help users maintain realistic mental models of end-to-end security without causing alert fatigue or unnecessary panic during routine key renewals.

### Data Retention, Ephemeral Messaging, and UX Nuance
At 23:40, Huerta explores the security benefits of ephemeral, disappearing messages. He notes that while encryption protects data in transit, endpoint compromise and subpoena requests threaten stored chat logs. Platforms that default to expiring messages dramatically reduce user exposure. However, he also points out UX edge cases, such as accidental data loss when migrating between mobile handsets or dealing with multi-device synchronization (discussed around 28:46).

### Designing Empathetic Privacy Software
Concluding the session, Huerta urges security engineers and UX designers to collaborate early in the development lifecycle. Usable encryption cannot be achieved by tacking graphic interfaces onto command-line tools. By designing empathetic, forgiving software that anticipates human cognitive limits, developers can create secure systems that protect vulnerable populations, journalists, and activists in real-world hostile environments.

talks.title: Privacy is Not An Add On:Designing for Privacy
talks.teaser: Privacy is Not An Add On:Designing for Privacy
talks.summary:
### Core Tenets of Privacy by Design
At 00:00, Alisha Kloc introduces the fundamental premise of Privacy by Design (PbD): privacy cannot be retrofitted or bolted onto a product after engineering is complete. She argues that waiting until feature release to evaluate privacy risks inevitably leads to architectural compromises, regulatory penalties, and user backlash. Integrating privacy into the initial system requirements allows organizations to build user trust while engineering compliant, resilient software.

### The Dangers of Unchecked Data Hoarding
At 05:12 and 10:30, Kloc critiques corporate data collection practices, challenging the pervasive Silicon Valley mindset that companies should capture and retain every possible telemetry point for hypothetical future use. She explains that every byte of stored user data represents an ongoing legal liability and a target for malicious hackers. Enforcing data minimization—collecting only the minimum data required to deliver immediate functionality—significantly lowers breach impact and operational risk.

### Contextual Consent vs. Deceptive Dark Patterns
At 15:16, the presentation examines user consent mechanisms, contrasting genuine, transparent user agency with deceptive "dark patterns." Kloc dissects examples from mainstream tech platforms (such as Google Now and smartphone operating systems) that bury tracking toggles within convoluted menus or use manipulative UI framing to coerce users into sharing location telemetry. True privacy design requires clear, plain-language notices presented contextually at the exact moment data is gathered.

### Anonymization, Pseudonymization, and Aggregation Pitfalls
At 21:40 and 26:15, Kloc explores the technical challenges of data sanitization. She warns against treating pseudonymization (like hashing email addresses or replacing names with UUIDs) as true anonymization. Citing real-world re-identification studies, she illustrates how adversaries easily correlate supposedly anonymized location trails, browser user-agent strings, or timestamped transaction logs with external public datasets to de-anonymize individual users.

### Operationalizing Privacy Engineering in Product Lifecycles
Concluding between 28:10 and 30:52, Kloc provides actionable guidance for engineering teams. She recommends integrating Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs) into sprint planning, establishing strict automated data retention and pruning jobs, segregating analytics databases from production user databases, and preparing engineering pipelines for emerging data protection regulations such as the European Union's GDPR.
